name: Apollo 16
short_status: Landed in the Descartes Highlands April 20, 1972; splashed down April 27, 1972 after a mission cut one day short.
tagline: NASA · United States · Crewed landing · 1972 · The space race Success

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 16 April 1972, 12:54 p.m. EST, Saturn V from Pad 39A, Kennedy Space Center

facts.label: Crew
facts.value: John W. Young (Commander), Thomas K. Mattingly II (Command Module Pilot, CSM Casper), Charles M. Duke Jr. (Lunar Module Pilot, LM Orion)

facts.label: Lunar landing
facts.value: 20 April 1972, about 9:24 p.m. EST, Descartes Highlands, 5 h 43 m behind schedule after an SPS backup-circuit yaw oscillation on the CSM

facts.label: Near-abort
facts.value: The SPS oscillation appeared during circularization prep on the 12th lunar revolution; Mission Control had roughly 10 hours to clear the landing before the orbital track drifted too far west

facts.label: LM coordinates (LROC-derived)
facts.value: 8.9734 S, 15.5011 E, uncertainty ±3.0 m, statistical mean of repeated LROC NAC imaging 2009-2015

facts.label: Surface stay
facts.value: 71 hours 2 minutes; three EVAs totaling 20 h 14 m (7:11 on Apr 21, 7:23 on Apr 22, 5:40 on Apr 23)

facts.label: Rover distance
facts.value: 16.6 miles (26.7 km) on the second Lunar Roving Vehicle, including the filmed 'Grand Prix' driving demonstration

facts.label: Samples
facts.value: 95.71 kg (211.00 lb), the official Lunar Receiving Laboratory total per NASA SP-4029 (NASA feature pages round to 209 lb); includes Big Muley at ~26 lb (11.7 kg), the largest single sample returned by any Apollo mission

facts.label: Science first
facts.value: George Carruthers' Far Ultraviolet Camera/Spectrograph, set up in Orion's shadow on EVA-1, was the first astronomical observatory operated on the Moon; it captured Earth's geocorona and still sits at the site

facts.label: Headline geology result
facts.value: Pre-mission consensus (site selected 17 June 1971) held that the Cayley plains and Descartes formations were volcanic; the returned rocks were impact breccias

facts.label: Breccia finding (primary literature)
facts.value: Apollo 16 geologic summary: the site is dominated by impact breccias derived from an anorthosite-gabbro complex; basalts are not their source

facts.label: Youngest moonwalker
facts.value: Charlie Duke, the tenth and youngest person to walk on the Moon (age 36), logging over 21 hours of EVA

facts.label: Early return
facts.value: Because of the SPS concern, Mission Control had the crew leave lunar orbit one day early; Mattingly performed a 1 h 23 m deep-space EVA on the way home to retrieve SIM-bay film, 197,000 miles from Earth

facts.label: Splashdown
facts.value: 27 April 1972, just before 3 p.m. EST, Pacific Ocean; total mission 265 h 51 m 5 s (11 days 1 h 51 m)

facts.label: 2025-2026 legacy
facts.value: NASA's Carruthers Geocorona Observatory, named for the Apollo 16 telescope's inventor, launched 24 September 2025 and began its 24-month primary science mission at Sun-Earth L1 on 1 March 2026

timeline: Descartes selected as the landing site, chosen largely to test the volcanic-highlands hypothesis
Launch at 12:54 p.m. EST from Pad 39A
SPS backup-loop yaw oscillation puts the landing in doubt; Orion touches down at Descartes about 9:24 p.m. EST, 5 h 43 m late
EVA-1 (7 h 11 m): ALSEP deployed, far-UV camera set up, Young's jump salute photographed by Duke
EVA-2 (7 h 23 m, then an Apollo record): 6.9-mile rover traverse; Big Muley collected
EVA-3 (5 h 40 m); Orion lifts off the Moon at 8:26 p.m. EST
Mattingly's 1 h 23 m trans-Earth EVA to retrieve SIM-bay film cassettes, on the crew's 10th day in space
Splashdown in the Pacific just before 3 p.m. EST; mission shortened by one day
Carruthers Geocorona Observatory, named for the Apollo 16 far-UV camera's inventor, launches with IMAP
Carruthers begins its 24-month primary science mission at L1, continuing the geocorona work Apollo 16 started
